これ は なん です か — What is this?
You point at things, ask what they are and how much they cost, and buy something. You meet katakana.
To point at things: これ / それ / あれ (this / that / that over there).
To use この / その / あの + noun.
To ask “what?” (なん) and “whose?” (だれ の).
To say “me too / this too” with も.
To buy something: 〜を ください, いくら です か, numbers up to 10,000.
To recognise words written in katakana.
Kenji takes Mihai to a small Japanese shop in Madrid. Mihai wants to try something new.
That’s senbei. It’s a Japanese snack.
Mihai, that one over there is good too, you know.
Then I’ll have that cake too, please.
Thank you very much. That’s eight euros in total.
Oh, look! Whose umbrella is this?
The line ー doubles the vowel before it: コーヒー = “koh-hee”, ケーキ = “keh-ki”. Hold the sound for two beats.
A small っ means a little pause, like a double consonant: まっちゃ = “mat-cha”, with a short stop before “cha”. Just like in Italian!
A small ゃ, ゅ or ょ joins the syllable before it: ひゃく = “hya-ku” (2 beats), ちゃ = “cha”.
1. これ / それ / あれ — like Spanish!
If you’ve learned Spanish, you’ll recognise the system: este / ese / aquel. Japanese has exactly the same three distances:
Remember the syllables: KO = near me, SO = near you, A = far away, DO = question. They come back in many words (ここ here, そこ there, あそこ over there, どこ where?).
2. この / その / あの + noun
これ / それ / あれ stand ALONE (“this”). When you want to say “THIS cake”, use この / その / あの before the noun.
This is good. / This cake is good.
Wrong: “これ ケーキ”. Correct: “この ケーキ”. And “この” can’t stand alone: “この は…” is wrong.
3. Questions: なん (what?) and だれ の (whose?)
The question word goes exactly where the answer would go. It doesn’t move to the front as in English.
When it’s clear what we’re talking about, the noun after の disappears: “わたし の です” = “It’s mine”. Just like English “mine”.
“What?” is なん (nan) before です and なに (nani) in many other situations. To begin with, use なん です か.
も (mo) takes the place of は and means “… too”, “also”.
You don’t use は and も together. “ゆきさん は も” is wrong: も replaces は (or を).
5. Shopping: をください and prices
“X を ください” = “X, please / Please give me X”. The most useful phrase in shops and restaurants.
Big numbers are built like on a calculator: 300 = “three hundred” = さん + ひゃく. A few change their pronunciation slightly:
Prices in Japan are in yen: 500 yen = ごひゃく えん (gohyaku en). A coffee costs about 400–500 yen.
6. Katakana: the alphabet of foreign words
コーヒー, ケーキ, ユーロ, パン… Words borrowed from other languages are written in katakana. The sounds are identical to hiragana; only the shapes differ: か = カ, こ = コ, け = ケ.
A useful game: read katakana words out loud and guess the foreign word! Many come from English: アイスクリーム = ice cream.
